title: Rectal pain in a 39-year-old barista
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 39-year-old barista in general practice with 4 days of severe anal pain that starts with each bowel motion, a small amount of bright red bleeding, and a background of constipation and hard stools. The candidate must ask about sensitive matters tactfully, rule out the other perianal causes, and gain consent for a perianal examination with a chaperone. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations and the perianal examination record and photograph. They must recognise an acute posterior midline anal fissure with no sentinel tag, and a separate long-standing skin tag that is incidental. They then plan conservative management, a sphincter relaxant if needed, safety netting and review.
focus: Anal pain on defecation: a focused, sensitive history, a perianal examination with consent, and general practice management of an anal fissure
stem: You are a GP registrar in an inner Sydney general practice. Peter Naser, a 39-year-old barista, has made an appointment because of pain in his back passage. A practice nurse is available to act as a chaperone.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Naser and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Naser's observations and the record of his perianal examination, with a photograph. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Peter Naser, a 39-year-old barista. You are embarrassed to be talking about your bottom and a little awkward at first, but you relax if the candidate puts you at ease. You sit gingerly, shifting your weight to one side. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "It's a bit embarrassing, but I've been getting this really bad pain in my backside."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Started about 4 days ago. Only if asked how it started: it came on after you passed a hard poo.
  • Now the pain starts every time you open your bowels and lasts a few hours, then settles until the next time. You have never had anything like it before.
  • Site: "Just around the opening of my back passage." It doesn't spread anywhere.
  • Character: sharp, like being cut, while you are going; duller and aching afterwards.
  • Severity: 10 out of 10 when you go. Right now, a few hours after this morning's bowel motion, it is a dull ache.
  • Worse when you open your bowels.
  • Anything that helps: "I can't think of anything specific."
  • Effect on you: "It's just so terrible when I try to go to the toilet. I just try to go as little as possible!"

Other symptoms (give only when asked):

  • Bleeding: bright red blood, about a teaspoon, when you go. It is on the toilet paper and on the outside of the poo, not mixed through it.
  • A lump: "There's a little bit of skin hanging down there, like a skin tag." It's been there for a year or two; it isn't new and doesn't hurt.
  • Bowels: you have always tended to be constipated. Your poos are hard and you have to strain.
  • Fluids, if asked: "I drink a lot of coffee at work. Probably not enough water."

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • A lump that comes down and goes back, or a hard, very tender lump that appeared suddenly. Itching. Discharge or mucus.
  • Swelling, throbbing pain that is there all the time, pus, fever or feeling unwell. Redness spreading over the skin.
  • Pain, swelling or discharge at the top of the crease of your buttocks.
  • Sudden brief attacks of pain in the back passage that wake you at night and have nothing to do with going to the toilet.
  • Weight loss, tiredness, diarrhoea, blood mixed in with the poo, black poo, a change in how often you go, or tummy pain.
  • Mouth ulcers, painful joints, red eyes or rashes.
  • Anyone in the family with bowel cancer or Crohn's disease or colitis.

Sexual history (only if asked, and more easily if the candidate explains why they are asking): one long-term partner. No anal sex. No symptoms of a sexually transmitted infection.

Past medical history: appendicectomy (appendix out) at 18. Coeliac disease, diagnosed at 23; you stick to a gluten-free diet.

Medications: none. You are not taking any pain killers, iron or anything else. Allergies: no medicine allergies. Intolerances: lactose intolerance. Vaccinations are up to date.

Family history: your mother was diagnosed with coeliac disease at 38. Your father is healthy.

Social history:

  • Barista. Lives with your partner and your dog in inner Sydney. You feel well connected and supported.
  • Smoke 5 cigarettes a day, for 20 years.
  • Alcohol: about 5 standard drinks each weekend.
  • Exercise: "I'd say that I'm quite fit. I run half marathons every month and I'm currently learning Muay Thai."
  • Diet: you limit sugar and greasy food and eat lots of protein. "I'm not a fan of my greens."

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "Not sure."
  • Concern: the pain is so bad that you are putting off going to the toilet.
  • Expectation: you want something to stop it hurting.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: well, alert, uncomfortable when sitting and shifts his weight. Not pale. Weight 72 kg.
  • Observations (10:05): temperature 36.8 °C, HR 92 regular, BP 128/80, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, pain 4/10 at rest.
  • Hands, eyes and mouth: no clubbing or pallor. No mouth ulcers.
  • Abdomen: healed appendicectomy scar in the right iliac fossa. Not distended. Soft and non-tender throughout, no masses, no palpable faecal loading, no hepatosplenomegaly. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Inguinal lymph nodes: not enlarged.
  • Perianal examination and digital rectal examination: only once the candidate has explained the examination, gained Peter's consent and offered a chaperone, say: "Peter agrees and the practice nurse is present as a chaperone. The findings of the perianal examination will be given to you in Part 2." If the candidate does not seek consent or offer a chaperone, Peter says: "Hang on, what are you going to do?"

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Peter's identity, gains consent for the consultation and reassures him about confidentiality.
Acknowledges his embarrassment, normalises the problem, stays non-judgemental and uses plain language (no unexplained jargon such as 'defecation' or 'PR').
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: around the anal opening, no radiation.
Onset and timing: began 4 days ago after passing a hard stool; comes with every bowel motion, lasts a few hours, then settles; never before.
Character and severity: sharp during the bowel motion, duller afterwards, 10/10.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with bowel motions, nothing helps, and he is putting off going to the toilet.

check.x: Asks about bleeding and characterises it: bright red, about a teaspoon, on the paper and the outside of the stool, not mixed through it.
Asks about bowel habit: long-standing constipation, hard stools and straining.
Asks cluster questions to rule out other perianal causes:
check.d: Award each kid for at least two relevant questions in that group.

kids.x: Haemorrhoids or perianal haematoma: a lump that prolapses or a sudden tender lump (he has noticed only a long-standing skin tag), itch, discharge.
Abscess, fistula, cellulitis or infected pilonidal sinus: constant throbbing pain, swelling, pus or discharge, fever, spreading redness, pain at the top of the natal cleft.
Proctalgia fugax: brief attacks of anal pain at night, unrelated to bowel motions.

check.x: Screens for red flags for colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease: weight loss, change in bowel habit, diarrhoea, blood mixed with the stool or melaena, abdominal pain, extraintestinal symptoms, and family history of bowel cancer or IBD.
check.d: Award for at least four of these.

check.x: Asks about risk factors:

kids.x: Diet and fluids: high protein, little fibre ('not a fan of my greens'), lots of coffee and not enough water.
Sexual history, including receptive anal sex, asked sensitively with an explanation of why it is relevant.

check.x: Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history: appendicectomy at 18, coeliac disease since 23 on a gluten-free diet, no medicines (including no constipating medicines), no medicine allergies (lactose intolerance), vaccinations up to date.
Takes a family history: mother has coeliac disease (diagnosed at 38), father healthy, no bowel cancer or IBD.
Takes a social history: barista, 5 cigarettes a day for 20 years, about 5 standard drinks each weekend, runs half marathons and does Muay Thai, lives with partner and dog, well supported.
check.d: Award for occupation, smoking quantified, alcohol and living situation.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, avoiding the toilet because of the pain, wants the pain to stop.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and inspects generally: notes he is afebrile with a heart rate of 92 and a normal BP, uncomfortable sitting, and not pale.
Examines the abdomen and inguinal nodes: appendicectomy scar, soft and non-tender, no masses or faecal loading, nodes not enlarged.

Explains the perianal examination and digital rectal examination in plain words, gains explicit consent, offers a chaperone, and describes the position (left lateral, knees drawn up, undressed from the waist down with a sheet).
States they would inspect the perianal skin and natal cleft first, part the buttocks gently, and not force a digital rectal examination if it is too painful.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: afebrile, heart rate settling from 92 to 80 as the pain eases, normal BP and saturations; he is systemically well, which argues against an abscess and supports care in general practice.
Identifies the linear split in the anoderm in the posterior midline (6 o'clock) as an anal fissure; a separate small long-standing skin tag at 11 o'clock is incidental, and there is no sentinel tag.

Notes the negative findings (no swelling, fluctuance, external fistula opening, thrombosed haemorrhoid or pilonidal sinus) and that the DRE was deferred because of pain and sphincter spasm, which itself supports a fissure.

States that a single posterior midline fissure is typical of a primary fissure, whereas a lateral, multiple or non-healing fissure needs a secondary cause excluded (such as Crohn's disease, an anal STI or cancer).

Gives the diagnosis as an acute primary anal fissure caused by hard stools and constipation, justified by pain with every bowel motion lasting hours, small bright red bleeding, and the examination findings.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:

kids.x: Thrombosed haemorrhoid or perianal haematoma: against: pain only with bowel motions and settling between them, no tender lump on inspection.
Perianal abscess or fistula: against: afebrile, no constant throbbing pain, swelling, fluctuance, discharge or external opening.

At least one of: proctalgia fugax (against: not brief or nocturnal), secondary fissure from Crohn's disease or an anal STI (against: single posterior midline fissure, no bowel symptoms, no anal sex or STI symptoms), anorectal cancer (against: short history, no red flags, bleeding explained by the fissure).

check.x: Management

Explains the diagnosis in plain words: a small tear in the lining of the back passage; the pain makes the ring muscle spasm, which cuts the blood supply and stops it healing, and avoiding the toilet makes the stools harder; most heal once the stools are soft.
Softens the stools:

kids.x: More dietary fibre and water (with extra fluid when running).
A bulk-forming laxative (for example psyllium) with plenty of water, adding a stool softener or osmotic laxative (for example macrogol) if the stools stay hard.
Goes to the toilet when he feels the urge rather than holding on, and avoids straining.

check.x: Relieves the pain: warm sitz baths after bowel motions, a topical local anaesthetic (for example lidocaine) for short-term use only (a few days to a couple of weeks), and paracetamol; avoids codeine because it constipates.
check.d: Award for sitz baths plus at least one of the other measures.

check.x: Offers a sphincter relaxant if the pain persists or the fissure is not healing:
check.d: Accept starting it now given the severity of his pain.

kids.x: Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% ointment (Rectogesic): about 1 cm of ointment applied with a gloved finger just inside the anal canal every 12 hours, for up to 8 weeks, explaining that it relaxes the spasm and restores blood flow so the tear can heal.
kids.d: Accept topical diltiazem 2% (compounded) as an alternative for this mark.

kids.x: Warns that headache is common and it can cause dizziness, and that it must not be used with sildenafil-type medicines (PDE5 inhibitors).

check.x: Answers his questions honestly: most fissures heal without an operation; he can keep training while keeping well hydrated.
Safety netting

Tells him to seek same-day review, or go to the ED, for constant throbbing pain, a swelling or lump, pus, fever or spreading redness, or heavy bleeding, clots or feeling faint; and to see the GP sooner if bleeding continues once the pain has settled, or for blood mixed in the stool or a change in bowel habit.
check.d: Award for at least three urgent red flags with where to go, plus persistent bleeding or a change in bowel habit as a reason to return.

check.x: Arranges GP review in 2 to 3 weeks with a rectal examination once less tender; colorectal referral (botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy) and a search for IBD if not healed by about 8 weeks or atypical.

part2.lead: Peter agreed to the examination, and the practice nurse was present as a chaperone. Here are his observations, a repeat set the nurse took afterwards, and the record of his perianal examination with a photograph.
part2.patient:
Ask these questions once each while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "Is this going to need an operation?"
  • "Can I keep running and doing Muay Thai?"

You are relieved that it is a small tear and nothing more serious. If the candidate uses jargon such as "fissure", "sphincter" or "sitz bath" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. First set on arrival; repeat set by the practice nurse after the examination. No medicines given.
handover.model:
• Read: general practice has no zoned chart, so read the values and the trend. Temperature 36.8 then 36.7 °C (afebrile). HR 92, settling to 80 as the pain eases. BP, RR and SpO2 normal. Pain 4/10 at rest, falling to 3/10.
  • For Peter: he is systemically well. The heart rate on arrival reflects pain from this morning's bowel motion. No fever, which argues against a perianal abscess or cellulitis.
  • What it changes: he can be managed in general practice. A fever, a rising heart rate or constant throbbing pain would mean reassessing for an abscess.

rows.note: On arrival; opened bowels about 3 hours ago

handover.label: Perianal examination record and photograph
handover.result:
Examination: perianal inspection, left lateral position with knees drawn up. Practice nurse present as chaperone. Verbal consent obtained.

Clinical details: 39-year-old man with 4 days of severe anal pain with each bowel motion, lasting hours; small-volume bright red bleeding; long-standing constipation with hard stools.

Findings:

  • Perianal skin: no erythema, induration, swelling or fluctuance. No external opening or discharge. No excoriation.
  • Natal cleft: no pits, sinus, swelling or discharge.
  • Anal verge (buttocks gently parted): a single short linear split in the anoderm in the posterior midline (6 o'clock by the lithotomy convention), running from the anal verge into the anal canal. The base is pink-red and clean; the edges are not raised or indurated, and no sphincter muscle fibres are visible in the base. No tag at the outer end of the fissure. A small soft, non-tender skin tag at the right anterior anal margin (11 o'clock by the lithotomy convention), away from the fissure; patient reports it is long-standing. No lateral or anterior splits.
  • Haemorrhoids: no prolapsed or thrombosed haemorrhoid; no tense bluish perianal lump.
  • Anal sphincter: visibly contracted on parting the buttocks.
  • Digital rectal examination: not performed. Gentle parting of the buttocks caused severe pain and the patient asked to stop. Proctoscopy not performed.

Summary: single posterior midline linear tear of the anoderm with clean edges and sphincter spasm; no sentinel tag. Separate incidental long-standing skin tag at the right anterior margin (11 o'clock), away from the fissure. No perianal swelling, discharge, external opening, haemorrhoid or natal cleft sinus. DRE deferred because of pain.
handover.model:
• Read: healthy perianal skin and natal cleft; a single linear split in the posterior midline with a clean base and soft edges; no tag at its outer end; a separate small long-standing skin tag at the right anterior margin (11 o'clock), away from the fissure; sphincter spasm; no abscess, fistula opening, thrombosed haemorrhoid or pilonidal sinus; DRE deferred because of pain.
  • For Peter: an acute primary anal fissure caused by hard stools; the anterior skin tag is incidental. The posterior midline is the typical site, so no secondary cause is suggested, and being too tender for a DRE itself supports a fissure. The fissure explains the bright red bleeding. No sentinel tag at the outer end of the fissure, no raised indurated edges and no exposed sphincter fibres, so this is acute; check that it heals.
  • What it changes: conservative management in general practice, with a DRE (and anoscopy if needed) once it is less tender. A lateral or multiple fissure, or one that does not heal, would need IBD and other causes excluded, with colorectal referral.

ask: You are now handing Peter over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Peter Naser, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Peter now, here in general practice.
Before Peter goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar; Peter Naser, 39, barista.
  • Situation: 4 days of severe anal pain with every bowel motion, small bright red bleeding; examination shows an anal fissure.
  • Background: began after a hard stool; long-standing constipation, straining, low-fibre diet. Coeliac disease (gluten-free), appendicectomy. Smokes 5 a day. No red flags.
  • Assessment: afebrile, HR 92 settling to 80, BP normal: systemically well. Single posterior midline tear with clean edges, no sentinel tag, and sphincter spasm, too tender for DRE; a separate incidental skin tag at 11 o'clock; no abscess, fistula, haemorrhoid or pilonidal sinus. Acute primary anal fissure.
  • Recommendation: manage here with stool softening and analgesia; plan as follows.

Most likely: acute primary anal fissure (posterior midline; no sentinel tag, raised edges or exposed sphincter fibres, so acute). Sharp pain with each bowel motion lasting hours after a hard stool, small bright red bleeding, constipation, the posterior midline tear, and too tender for a DRE. The skin tag at 11 o'clock is separate and incidental.

  • Thrombosed haemorrhoid or perianal haematoma: for: onset after straining. Against: pain settles between motions, no tender lump.
  • Perianal abscess or fistula: against: afebrile, no swelling, discharge or external opening.
  • Secondary fissure (Crohn's disease, anal STI): against: posterior midline, single, no bowel or extraintestinal symptoms, no anal sex or STI symptoms.
  • Others: proctalgia fugax (against: not brief or nocturnal); anorectal cancer (against: short history, no red flags).

1. Explain the tear and the pain-spasm cycle in plain words.
  2. Soften the stools: more fibre and water; a bulk-forming laxative (psyllium), adding macrogol if still hard. Go when he feels the urge; do not hold on or strain.
  3. Pain relief: warm sitz baths after bowel motions, a topical local anaesthetic for short-term use only, paracetamol. Avoid codeine.
  4. If needed, relax the sphincter: GTN 0.2% ointment (Rectogesic), about 1 cm applied with a gloved finger just inside the anal canal every 12 hours for up to 8 weeks (headache common, dizziness; not with sildenafil-type medicines), or topical diltiazem 2%.
  5. Chronic or non-healing: colorectal referral for botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy; exclude IBD.
  6. His questions: most heal without surgery; he can keep training with good hydration.

• Same-day review or the ED for constant throbbing pain, a swelling or lump, pus, fever or spreading redness (abscess), or heavy bleeding, clots or feeling faint.
  • See the GP sooner if bleeding continues once the pain settles, or for blood mixed in the stool, a change in bowel habit, diarrhoea, weight loss or tummy pain.
  • Stop the GTN and seek advice if headaches or dizziness are severe.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 3 weeks to check healing, with a rectal examination once less tender; colorectal referral (botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy) and a search for IBD if not healed by about 8 weeks or if atypical. Written information on diet and laxatives.

ddx.for: Sharp pain with every bowel motion lasting hours since a hard stool, small bright red bleeding, constipation, a posterior midline tear with clean edges and no sentinel tag, and too tender for a DRE.

ddx.dx: Thrombosed external haemorrhoid or perianal haematoma
ddx.for: Sudden painful onset after straining with a hard stool, bright red bleeding and a perianal skin lump.
ddx.against: Pain comes only with bowel motions and settles between them, and there is no tense, tender bluish lump on inspection.
Pain is episodic rather than constant and throbbing, he is afebrile, and there is no swelling, fluctuance, discharge or external opening.

ddx.for: Severe, sharp anal pain in a young adult.
ddx.against: His pain is triggered by bowel motions and lasts hours, with no brief nocturnal attacks.

ddx.dx: Secondary anal fissure (Crohn's disease, anal STI such as syphilis or herpes, HIV)
ddx.for: He has an autoimmune bowel disease (coeliac disease), as does his mother.
ddx.against: Single posterior midline fissure; one long-term partner, no anal sex or STI symptoms; no diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain or extraintestinal features.
Short history with bleeding on the paper explained by the fissure, no change in bowel habit, weight loss or family history.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the first set of observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, give findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The perianal findings are given in Part 2: in Part 1, mark only how the candidate explains the perianal examination and DRE, gains consent and offers a chaperone. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the examination findings will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over both results (with the photograph if available), then ask the four questions in order. Peter asks his two questions once each during the management answer.

Credit the differential clusters (haemorrhoids or perianal haematoma, abscess or fistula, cellulitis, infected pilonidal sinus, proctalgia fugax) when the candidate asks targeted questions about them in the history or names them with a reason in Part 2.

A high-performing candidate puts Peter at ease, characterises the pain and links it to bowel motions, asks about bleeding and constipation, screens the other perianal causes and the bowel cancer and IBD red flags, takes a sexual history sensitively, and seeks consent for a chaperoned perianal examination. In Part 2 they recognise an acute posterior midline fissure with no sentinel tag and a separate incidental skin tag, and explain why its site matters. They plan stool softening, sitz baths, analgesia and a sphincter relaxant with the GTN warnings, and give clear red flags and a review.

A borderline candidate calls it haemorrhoids, insists on a DRE despite the pain, prescribes codeine, omits the GTN warnings, or gives no plan for a fissure that does not heal or bleeding that persists.
explain:
Diagnosis

Peter has an acute primary anal fissure: a linear tear in the anoderm of the distal anal canal, in the posterior midline. He also has a separate, long-standing skin tag at the right anterior margin, away from the fissure, which is incidental. The history is typical. Severe sharp pain started after a hard stool. It now comes with every bowel motion and lasts a few hours afterwards, with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, in a man who is constipated and strains. On examination there is a posterior midline tear, and he is too tender for a digital rectal examination, which itself supports a fissure.

Why fissures persist

The pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter. Spasm raises anal pressure and reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm, which stops the tear healing. Fear of the pain leads to holding on, which makes the stools harder and tears it again. Treatment breaks this cycle by softening the stools and relaxing the sphincter.

Primary and secondary fissures

  • Primary fissures occur in young and middle-aged adults after hard stools, or after receptive anal sex. About 90% are in the posterior midline (6 o'clock).
  • Secondary fissures occur with Crohn's disease, anal STIs (syphilis, herpes), HIV, TB and anal cancer. A fissure that is lateral, multiple, or chronic (persisting beyond about 6 to 8 weeks) needs a cause looked for.
  • Skin tags: a tag at the outer end of a fissure (a sentinel tag or pile) is a sign of a chronic fissure. Peter's tag is long-standing and lies at 11 o'clock, away from the fissure, so it is incidental. There is no sentinel tag at the outer end of the fissure, no raised indurated edges and no exposed sphincter fibres, so this is acute; check that it heals.

Differentials that matter

  • Thrombosed haemorrhoids or perianal haematoma: constant pain, an obvious tense, tender (often bluish) lump; bleeding only if it ulcerates.
  • Perianal abscess or fistula: constant throbbing pain, swelling, fever, discharge or an external opening. An abscess needs drainage.
  • Perianal cellulitis and infected pilonidal sinus: spreading redness, or pain and discharge at the top of the natal cleft.
  • Proctalgia fugax: brief, severe attacks of anal pain, often at night, unrelated to bowel motions.
  • Bowel cancer and IBD: screen for weight loss, change in bowel habit, diarrhoea, blood mixed with the stool and a family history. Rectal bleeding that continues after a fissure heals needs further investigation.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: afebrile and haemodynamically normal, with a heart rate that settles as the pain eases. He is systemically well, which argues against an abscess.
  • Perianal examination: a single posterior midline tear with a clean base and sphincter spasm, and no sentinel tag. There is a separate incidental skin tag away from the fissure, and no abscess, fistula, haemorrhoid or pilonidal sinus. This is a typical acute primary fissure.

Management (eTG Gastrointestinal: anal fissure)

  • Soften the stools: more dietary fibre and fluid, and a bulk-forming laxative (for example psyllium) with plenty of water; add a stool softener or osmotic laxative if the stools stay hard. Advise him not to hold on or strain.
  • Pain relief: warm sitz baths after bowel motions relax the sphincter. A topical local anaesthetic, for short-term use only (a few days to a couple of weeks), can give relief. Use paracetamol; avoid codeine, which constipates.
  • Sphincter relaxants, if needed: glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% ointment (Rectogesic) relaxes the spasm and restores blood flow. About 1 cm of ointment is applied with a gloved finger just inside the anal canal every 12 hours, for up to 8 weeks. Headache is common, and it can cause dizziness; it must not be used with PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil. Topical diltiazem 2% (compounded) is an alternative with fewer headaches.
  • Chronic or non-healing fissure: refer to a colorectal surgeon for botulinum toxin injection or lateral internal sphincterotomy, and look for a cause such as IBD.
  • Review: check healing, and do a DRE (and anoscopy if needed) once it is less tender.
  • General: his half marathons make hydration matter. Smoking cessation supports his general health.

Explaining a DRE to Peter

Check his understanding and explain in small chunks without jargon. Reassure him that he can stop the examination at any time, and offer a chaperone.

  • Indications: rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, anal pain, urinary or sexual symptoms in men (prostate), incontinence.
  • Procedure, before: a chaperone; undress from the waist down with a sheet for cover; lie on the left side with the knees drawn up.
  • Procedure, during: inspect the skin; ask him to cough and strain; insert a lubricated gloved finger gently; feel for masses, ulcers and the prostate; ask him to squeeze; check the glove for blood or mucus.
  • Procedure, after: offer tissues to clean up, and time to dress in private.
  • Benefits: quick, gives useful information. Risks: low; uncomfortable; a small risk of bleeding; latex allergy.
  • Alternatives: deferring the examination until it is less tender (as here), or examination under anaesthesia if needed.
  • Documentation: gain explicit consent, and record the consent, the chaperone and the findings.

Safety netting

He should seek same-day review or go to the ED for constant throbbing pain, a lump or swelling, pus, fever or spreading redness, or heavy bleeding or feeling faint. He should see his GP sooner if bleeding continues once the pain has settled, or if he notices blood mixed in the stool, a change in bowel habit, weight loss or abdominal pain. Arrange a review in 2 to 3 weeks, and refer to a colorectal surgeon if the fissure has not healed by about 8 weeks.
points: Anal fissure pain is sharp during a bowel motion and lasts minutes to hours afterwards, often with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, after a hard stool.
Pain causes internal sphincter spasm, which reduces blood flow and stops healing; avoiding the toilet makes the stools harder. Treatment breaks this cycle.
About 90% of primary fissures are in the posterior midline. A lateral, multiple or chronic fissure needs a secondary cause (such as Crohn's disease) excluded.
Being too tender for a DRE supports a fissure: inspect gently with consent and a chaperone, and do not force a DRE.

First-line care is soft stools (fibre, fluid, a bulk-forming laxative), warm sitz baths and topical analgesia, avoiding codeine. If needed, add GTN 0.2% ointment (headache common, not with PDE5 inhibitors) or topical diltiazem 2%.
A chronic fissure is referred for botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy, and bleeding that continues after healing needs investigation.
